title: Plantar Heel Pain (Plantar Fasciopathy)
case: Case: A 45-year-old nurse has 3 months of sharp pain under the left heel with her first steps in the morning, easing after a few minutes but returning at the end of a shift. She increased her walking recently and wears thin flat shoes. Tenderness is at the inner edge of the heel, the windlass test reproduces her pain, and the squeeze test is negative. Sensation is normal.

Working diagnosis: plantar fasciopathy. Plan: education, supportive cushioned shoes, plantar fascia and calf stretching, a progressive high-load heel raise program, taping or an orthosis for the start if helpful, and review in 3 to 4 weeks.
qa: Why is the heel spur on X-ray not the explanation? Spurs are common in people without pain and many people with plantar heel pain have no spur, so the pain is not explained by the spur itself [Ref - to verify].

Why is first-step pain typical? The fascia shortens and stiffens at rest and gets loaded suddenly on standing, which provokes pain until it warms up. This explanation is accepted but not fully proven.
A runner has pain with impact and a positive squeeze test. What now? Suspect a calcaneal stress fracture, stop loading and refer for imaging.
Why use heel raises rather than only stretching? A trial found that high-load strengthening gave better outcomes than stretching alone [Ref - to verify].
Why is repeated steroid injection discouraged? There is a risk of fat pad thinning and fascia rupture and long-term benefit is limited [Ref - to verify].

fields.Purpose: Tighten the plantar fascia by extending the big toe to see whether it reproduces the heel pain
fields.Patient position: Standing with weight on both feet (weight-bearing version), or sitting with the foot relaxed and the ankle in neutral (non-weight-bearing version)
fields.Therapist position: Kneeling in front of the foot
fields.Action: Passively extend (dorsiflex) the big toe at the joint while the ankle stays still. Hold for up to about 30 seconds and ask about heel pain
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar heel pain
fields.Negative: No pain or only a stretch sensation at the toe
fields.Supports: Plantar fasciopathy, mainly when combined with local tenderness
fields.Limits: Reported accuracy varies, and the weight-bearing version may be more sensitive. A negative test does not exclude the condition [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Moving the ankle during the test; forcing the toe too far; counting toe-joint pain as positive
fields.Next step: If positive, check calf flexibility and begin the fasciopathy plan

tests.name: Palpation of the medial calcaneal tubercle

fields.Action: Press firmly on the inner side of the underside of the heel bone and along the first part of the fascia
fields.Positive: Localised tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain
fields.Limits: A tender heel pad or stress fracture may also be tender, so combine with other findings

fields.Action: Squeeze the heel bone from both sides with both hands
fields.Supports: Calcaneal stress fracture rather than plantar fasciopathy; refer for imaging

redFlags.Finding: Sudden tearing pain with a pop and swelling or bruising
redFlags.Immediate action: Protect; refer if severe or unable to bear weight

redFlags.Finding: Squeeze test positive or pain with impact in a runner or after a rise in training
Hot, red, swollen heel with fever
Diabetes with an open wound or loss of sensation
Constant night pain, weight loss, swelling or a lump
Bilateral heel pain with morning stiffness, other joints, eye or skin changes

manual.name: Soft-tissue work (calf, plantar fascia region)
manual.why: Short-term comfort and flexibility [Ref - to verify]
manual.application: Gentle sustained pressure; ball or foam roller for self-treatment

manual.name: Talocrural or first-ray mobilization
manual.why: Improves ankle dorsiflexion or toe movement

manual.name: Dry needling or other invasive techniques
manual.application: Only within scope and with caution

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and a loading program. Manual therapy is an optional short-term adjunct and does not replace exercise. Do not claim that manual therapy removes a heel spur or breaks down the fascia.

exercise.Steps: Sit, cross the foot over the knee, pull the toes
back until you feel a stretch in the arch
exercise.Starting dose: daily; start before getting out of bed

exercise.Steps: Lean into a wall with the back leg straight, then bent

exercise.Exercise: High-load heel raise with a rolled towel under the toes
exercise.Steps: Stand with the toes lifted on a rolled towel, rise onto the toes slowly (about 3 seconds up, 2-second pause, 3 seconds down)
exercise.Starting dose: 3 sets, starting at about 12 reps and reducing as load increases, 3 days a week [Ref - to verify]
exercise.Progress when: Pain 4 out of 10 or less; add a backpack for load
exercise.Regress when: Pain above 5 out of 10 or lasting into the next day

exercise.Steps: Draw the ball of the foot toward the heel without curling the toes

exercise.Comment: Avoid thin flat shoes and barefoot walking on hard floors in the early weeks

exercise.When to consider: Short-term pain relief, especially with a high or low arch or a trial to off-load the heel
exercise.Comment: Benefit is modest and mostly short term [Ref - to verify]
Use to allow activity; effect is temporary [Ref - to verify]
Evidence is limited and comfort varies [Ref - to verify]

exerciseNotes: Principle: a plan combining education, loading of the plantar fascia and calf, stretching, and footwear or orthosis support is generally used. High-load strengthening has shown benefit over stretching alone in at least one trial [Ref - to verify]. Effects of different treatments are often modest, and recovery is gradual.
Symptom rule: pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within 24 hours is acceptable. First-step pain the next morning should not become much worse.

Load management: reduce, rather than stop, painful activities (long standing, hard surfaces, barefoot walking, running distance). Replace some running with cycling or swimming for a time and build running back gradually.

modalities.name: Cold (rolling the foot over a frozen bottle)
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy
modalities.indicated: Option for persistent pain after several months of care
modalities.comment: Evidence is mixed and depends on the dose [Ref - to verify]

modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with risks such as fat pad thinning and fascia rupture, so it is used with caution [Ref - to verify]. Other injections and surgery are for persistent cases after a long course of non-surgical care.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Heel pain with first-step morning pain, tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle, a positive windlass test, and a negative squeeze test? Yes: working diagnosis is plantar fasciopathy.
Burning or tingling? Yes: consider nerve entrapment.
Squeeze positive? Yes: consider stress fracture and refer.
If typical, start education, load management and strengthening; add stretching, footwear and an orthosis based on the patient's response.
If no improvement after a suitable trial, review the diagnosis and consider medical options.
Visit 1: screen flags, confirm the diagnosis, explain the condition and its usual course, start load management and a home program.
Early: reduce painful loading, supportive footwear, stretch and begin heel raises, optional taping or orthosis.
